paragraphs.text: SHAHID BILAL HASSAN, J- The present appeals arise out of a suit for pre-emption instituted by the respondent (Muhammad Azam) in respect of a transaction relating to the suit property. The learned Trial Court, upon appraisal of the evidence, dismissed the suit. The learned Appellate Court, however, reversed the said decree and decreed the suit, which judgment was maintained by the learned High Court in revision. Against the judgement of the High Court a Civil Petition for Leave to appeal before this Court was preferred in which leave has already been granted. Hence, this appeal. C.A. No. 28-L/2011 etc.

Learned counsel for the appellant submits that the transaction embodied in the impugned mutation was one of exchange (badal) and not a sale, therefore, no right of pre-emption accrued in favour of the respondent. It is further contended that even otherwise the respondent failed to prove the mandatory requirements of pre-emption as the alleged notice of Talb-i-Ishhad was not proved in accordance with law, the postman was never produced to establish its service, and the respondent also failed to disclose the source from which he acquired knowledge of the sale consideration.
We have heard the learned counsel for the parties and have examined the record.

The primary question is whether the impugned transaction constituted a sale or an exchange. The mutation and the attendant circumstances unmistakably demonstrate that the parties had exchanged their respective properties. It is by now well settled that the right of pre-emption is a weak right and constitutes a restriction upon an owner's freedom to alienate his property; consequently, the provisions creating such a right must receive strict construction. Since the right of pre-emption arises only where the impugned transaction is a sale, the burden squarely rests upon the pre-emptor to establish that the transaction, notwithstanding its form, was in reality a sale. In the absence of convincing evidence to discharge such burden, the suit must fail. The recent judgment of this Court reported as Muhammad Mushtaq and others v. Malik Mutaz through L.Rs. and others (2026 SCMR 54) has reiterated that where the transaction recorded in the mutation is an exchange, no right of pre- emption arises, and if any ambiguity exists regarding the true nature of the transaction, the Courts ought not to presume it to be a sale.

In the present case, the respondent has failed to produce any credible evidence establishing payment or promise of consideration so as to convert the transaction of exchange into a sale. The Courts below misdirected themselves by shifting the burden upon the defendants instead of requiring the plaintiff to affirmatively prove that the transaction was a sale. Their findings, therefore, cannot be sustained in law. C.A. No. 28-L/2011 etc.

Even otherwise, in order to do complete justice between the parties, we have independently examined the evidence on record and find that the respondent has failed to establish compliance with the mandatory requirements governing a suit for pre-emption. The alleged notice of Talb-i-Ishhad was not proved in accordance with law. The postman, who allegedly effected service of the registered notice, was never produced despite specific denial by the defendants. It is settled by this Court in Allah Ditta through L.Rs. v. Muhammad Anar (2013 SCMR 866) and reaffirmed in Dayam Khan v. Muslim Khan (2015 SCMR 222) that where service of Talb-i- Ishhad is disputed, production of the postman is indispensable and failure to examine him is fatal to the pre-emptor's case.

We further notice that the respondent also failed to disclose the source from which he acquired knowledge of the alleged sale consideration. Such omission goes to the root of the matter because a pre-emptor must establish lawful knowledge of the transaction and its consideration before asserting the statutory right. In Subhanuddin v. Pir Ghulam (PLD 2015 SC 69), this Court held that a pre-emptor cannot merely state the sale price without disclosing the source of such information, as such conduct is inconsistent with the principles governing the law of pre-emption.

For the foregoing reasons, this appeal is allowed. The judgments and decrees passed by the learned High Court and the learned Appellate Court are set aside. Consequently, the judgment and decree of the learned Trial Court dismissing the suit are restored, albeit for reasons different from those assigned therein. The suit for pre-emption filed by the respondent accordingly stands dismissed. JUDGE JUDGE Lahore, the 27th of July, 2026 “Approved for Reporting” M.A. Hassan
